name: Jade Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you say is confidential. What is a usual workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade Khan, 58, and I took my vocational certificate after years in a warehouse and raising our children. Now I help build and repair power lines for an electricity company; I'm paid well but still junior, and Ruth checks my difficult tie-offs before I climb.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is hard about being junior at this age?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I know how to work, but these circuits are new to me. A twisted strap by the canal bridge reminded me to take correction without pride getting in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a tidy form is no great revolution. We still put on the gloves, test the circuit and mend the actual wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, a slow outcome would be welcome. I came to line work after raising our children and years in a warehouse, and although this job pays well, I'm still the one asking for a second look at my tie-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking supervised repair jobs and spend one Saturday each month reviewing the certificate manual with my crew lead. In the first year I'll leave our eight months of savings untouched for real trouble and keep our usual household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the job. My husband Amir has steady cleaning work at the hospital, our children are grown, and we can pay our bills without a new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a second look catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew lead Ruth spotted a twisted strap before I climbed beside the canal bridge. My crew lead Ruth caught a twisted climbing strap before it could hurt me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever use AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I never have. If I need a practice question, I ask Ruth or open the training book, because I want to see the approved answer.

say: I'd say **circuit testing** and repair remain human jobs in this picture.
I'd call **tidier forms** useful but modest.
think: My **junior field skill** still needs a second set of eyes.
Our **eight-month reserve** and higher wage make the quiet outcome comfortable.
do: Keep **supervised repair jobs** and review the certificate manual monthly with Ruth.
Maintain the **usual budget** and leave emergency savings untouched in the first year.
feel: **Settled** about paid work and household bills.
S0.quote: My crew lead Ruth caught a twisted climbing strap before it could hurt me.
fieldNote: Jade's **late entry** and twisted-strap incident keep her humble about safety despite a higher pay rate.
She **never uses AI** and has enough savings to continue learning through Ruth and the approved manual.

steps.text: Continue supervised line repairs and monthly manual review with Ruth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office that buying software may speed up fittings, but our storekeeper should still check what's in the bin. I'd also say anyone whose desk job shrinks deserves honest notice, not a cheerful slogan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think a robot will be cleaning hospital rooms or climbing our poles tomorrow, so Amir's and my wages look fairly safe. I do wonder whether faster scheduling will trim our weekend callouts, which helped us build the savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the crew lead to show me the printed route beside the new dispatch suggestion after they have tested it. In the first year I'd keep taking repair shifts, and if weekend pay drops twice, Amir and I would delay replacing our dining table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about losing some extra hours and about the office people losing more. I can accept a proved route; I won't learn a screen just to make a manager happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide a route is proved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would compare the suggested road with the access key list and the actual feeder number. If the road is wrong, the software goes back to dispatch before the truck leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the dining table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old one is scratched but sound. The replacement money can sit in the bank while we see what happens to weekend callouts.

say: I'd ask for **storekeeper checks** before buying software changes staffing.
I'd demand **honest notice** for desk staff if posts shrink.
think: Our **base field wages** look safe while robots spread slowly.
My **weekend callouts** could fall as scheduling improves.
do: Compare **tested routes** with access keys and feeder numbers before leaving the depot.
Keep **repair shifts** and delay the dining table after two lost weekend pay periods.
feel: **Uneasy** about extra hours and office colleagues' jobs.
S1.quote: The old one is scratched but sound.
fieldNote: Jade expects **physical work to continue** for now, but sees plausible loss of the callouts that built her reserve.
Her **table purchase** is the first discretionary expense she would delay, while Ruth checks routes against real access details.

steps.text: Keep paid repair shifts and check routes with Ruth
Delay replacing the dining table after two lower weekend pay periods

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that thinking AI in 2028 doesn't let anyone skip a human isolation check. Field robots arriving around 2031 are the part that could cost us line jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 in 2031, and I might still need my pay even with eight months saved. Amir cleans hospital rooms, so capable robots could reach his hands-on work too; our grown children can help us find information, but they have homes of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask payroll for written retirement figures and ask Ruth what other line employers nearby require. In 2029 I'd apply to the municipal utility if our employer announces crew cuts; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd keep seeking paid repair or equipment-checking shifts and ask my brother to tell me about genuine openings at his firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel scared of both wages changing in the same year, though I know where to start asking. Savings buy us months to search, not a new career by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother works in a depot office, and I'd ask him to send the job notice, pay and requirements, not put in a word I haven't earned. I want work I can do safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the utility offered a paid equipment-checking course with a recognised certificate, I'd enrol. I won't spend our emergency savings on an unknown private school.

say: I'd insist on **human isolation checks** after 2028 thinking AI.
I'd say **2031 robots** could affect both line repairs and hospital cleaning.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when field robots arrive.
Amir's **cleaning income** could face the same robot date, making our reserve finite.
do: Request **written retirement figures** and check local utility requirements now.
Apply for **municipal line work** if cuts are announced; seek paid repair or equipment-checking shifts in 2031.
feel: **Scared** about two wages, with a concrete search plan.
S2.quote: Savings buy us months to search, not a new career by themselves.
fieldNote: Jade identifies **simultaneous hands-on risk** for her line job and Amir's hospital cleaning when robots arrive in 2031.
Her **family support** means job information, not expecting grown children or a brother to finance her household.

steps.text: Request retirement figures and check municipal utility requirements
Apply for municipal line work if her company announces crew cuts
Enrol in equipment-checking training if wages and certificate are provided
Ask her brother for real depot vacancy notices and requirements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train the crews and write safety rules before the machines reach our hands. Thinking AI comes in 2031, and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I may be able to retire, but I won't make that promise before Amir and I see what our actual income would be. His hospital cleaning job could face robots in the same year, so there may be no second wage to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request our retirement statements and keep learning safe line work with Ruth. In 2032 I'd pay a little extra off the home loan from my higher wage, and in the first robot year I'd either retire if our budget works or apply for paid meter-service work at one of the nearby utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to prepare than in the fast picture. The extra years are useful, but a shared robot date for our jobs still sits on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra on the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for sixty from each regular pay packet after our food and heating are covered. We would not empty the eight-month reserve to make the balance look pretty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why meter service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already help check seals after repairs, and it would be a smaller climb. I don't assume the vacancy will stay human after 2034, so I'd apply only when a real job is posted.

say: I'd use **five years** for crew training and safety rules.
I'd note **2031 thinking AI** comes before 2034 field robots.
think: At **66**, retirement needs a verified budget for both partners.
Amir's **hospital cleaning wage** could also change at the robot date.
do: Request **retirement statements** and keep learning field safety with Ruth.
Pay **sixty per pay packet** toward the home loan, then retire or apply for meter service in 2034.
feel: **More prepared**, though still concerned about both wages.
S3.quote: We would not empty the eight-month reserve to make the balance look pretty.
fieldNote: Jade treats **retirement at 66** as a conditional budget decision while both hands-on jobs face the 2034 robot date.
She would **reduce debt from wages**, preserving the reserve and looking for an actual meter-service posting if needed.

steps.text: Continue paid field practice with Ruth during the preparation years
Pay sixty from each regular pay packet toward the home loan
Compare both retirement statements with household costs before leaving work
Apply for posted meter-service work in 2034 if retirement falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger workers to learn a trade they can explain, not just push buttons. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, then field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to be retired from the pole before 71 if the figures agree with our bills. Amir would be older too, and his cleaning job might end before we planned, so we need a budget that does not rely on endless shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep taking paid repairs and request updated retirement figures each year. In 2037 Amir and I would settle on a retirement date if our home costs and medical bills fit; by the first robot year I'd hand Ruth my annotated circuit book for the younger apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my wages for the next few years. I also feel responsible for leaving clear lessons. Someone once took time to check my strap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is written in that circuit book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I marked the canal bridge access gate and the place where the pole tag is hard to read. An apprentice can check the paper against the site before trusting a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early just to avoid machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd choose the date from money and health, not a headline. Our grown children can visit and help with errands, but I wouldn't make them our income plan.

say: I'd urge apprentices to learn **explainable field skills** over the decade.
I'd name **2039 field robots** as the change when I'll be 71.
think: I may leave **pole work** before robots arrive if our numbers hold.
Amir's **cleaning income** also needs a cautious retirement forecast.
do: Keep **paid repairs** and update retirement figures each year.
Choose a **2037 date** if household bills fit, then pass the annotated circuit book to Ruth.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, responsible for apprentices' safety.
S4.quote: Someone once took time to check my strap.
fieldNote: Jade's likely **retirement before 2039** depends on both partners' costs and income, not age alone.
Her **annotated circuit book** is an apprenticeship handover tied to the corrected strap and local access hazards.

steps.text: Continue paid repairs and update retirement figures annually
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if household and medical costs fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots reach both my repair work and Amir's cleaning job around 2031. Written staffing plans, paid recognised training, real local openings and enough notice for both of us would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether older apprentices get the same chance to finish learning before a machine is bought. A late start is still honest work.

headlineQuote: A late start is still honest work.
portrait: Jade is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered after warehouse work and raising children, and still asks Ruth to inspect difficult tie-offs.
Her **eight-month reserve** provide room, while Amir's hospital cleaning is another hands-on job exposed to robots.
She **never uses AI tools** and learns from approved manuals, supervised practice and family-shared job information.
The **2031 robot date** worries her most because both household wages could change before retirement is affordable.
With longer warning, she **reduces home debt** from wages and checks retirement figures before choosing when to leave field work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Jade most because field robots in 2031 could affect both her work and Amir's cleaning wage.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **staffing notice**, paid recognised training and real local vacancies for both workers.
